## Some vectors

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse) # Add the tidyverse package to my current library.
library(haven) # Read and handle SPSS, Stata & SAS data (no need to install)
```

```{r}
# Import the ALLBUS 2025 data on gender attitudes,
# which you have downloaded into your data folder.
genderdata <- read_rds("../data/genderdata.rds")
```

```{r}
#| include: false
# Now create a couple of vectors, similar to
# the variables in the ALLBUS gender data.
(age <- c(52, 51, 32, 60, 76))
(sex <- factor(x = c("Mann", "Frau", "Frau", "Frau", "Frau"),
               levels = c("Mann", "Frau", "Divers")))
(eastwest <- factor(x = c("West", "West", "Ost", "West", "West"),
                    levels = c("West", "Ost")))
(incc <- c(2000, 1800, 950, 1300, 1300))
(id03 <- c(6, 6, 6, 5, 8))
```

```r

```

## Data frames

**Data frames** organize vectors of *equal length* along their indices.

```{r}
#| include: false
# Bind our 5 vectors along their index into a data frame.
# Assign that data frame to object "Dat".
(Dat <- data.frame(sex, age, eastwest, incc, id03))
```

```r
# Bind our 5 vectors along their index into a data frame.
# Assign that data frame to object "Dat".
(Dat <- data.frame(sex, age, eastwest, incc, id03))
```

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
Dat
```
:::

## Index (Rows, and columns)

In contrast to vectors, data frames and tibbles have rows and columns. As in matrix algebra, R's index thus distinguishes `[rows, columns]`. The `,` after `"Ost"` tells R that we talk about rows. To understand how the index method works, remember logical vectors:

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| include: false
# Print factor eastwest contained in tibble Dat.
Dat$eastwest

# Return a logical vector of whether the different
# elements in Dat$eastwest equal "Ost".
Dat$eastwest == "Ost"

# Feed the logical vector to the index of Dat
# to select TRUE cases living in Ost.
(Dat_small <- Dat[Dat$eastwest == "Ost", ])
```

```r
# Print factor eastwest contained in tibble Dat.
Dat$eastwest

# Return a logical vector of whether the different
# elements in Dat$eastwest equal "Ost".
Dat$eastwest == "Ost"

# Feed the logical vector to the index of Dat
# to select TRUE cases living in Ost.
(Dat_small <- Dat[Dat$eastwest == "Ost", ])
```

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
Dat$eastwest
Dat$eastwest == "Ost"
Dat_small
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
. . .

```{r}
#| include: false
# Create a new logical variable called "selector",
# which identifies cases living in Ost in Dat$eastwest.
Dat$selector <- Dat$eastwest == "Ost"

# Print Dat.
Dat
```

```r
# Create a new logical variable called "selector",
# which identifies cases living in Ost in Dat$eastwest.
```

## Transform, recode & generate (Variables of tibbles)

To transform and recode simply use `$` to clarify which tibble you are referring to.

```{r}
#| include: false
# Center age around the average age.
(Dat$age <- Dat$age - mean(Dat$age))
```

```r
# Center age around the average age.
(Dat$age <- Dat$age - mean(Dat$age))
```

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
Dat$age
```
:::

```{r}
#| include: false
# Recode "Ost" to "Neue Bundeslaender".
(Dat$eastwest <- fct_recode(Dat$eastwest, "Neue Bundeslaender" = "Ost"))
```

```r
# Recode "Ost" to "Neue Bundeslaender".
(Dat$eastwest <- fct_recode(Dat$eastwest, "Neue Bundeslaender" = "Ost"))
```

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
Dat$eastwest
```
:::

If you rather want to generate a new variable, just give it a name.

```{r}
#| include: false
# Devide age by its standard deviation;
# now it is z-standardized (mean = 0, sd = 1).
(Dat$z_age <- Dat$age / sd(Dat$age))
```

```r
# Devide age by its standard deviation;
# now it is z-standardized (mean = 0, sd = 1).
(Dat$z_age <- Dat$age / sd(Dat$age))
```

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
Dat$z_age
```
:::

## Transform, recode & generate (Several variables of a tibble)

If you want to transform and recode several variables from the same tibble, get used to use `mutate()`.
::: {.note}
You will better understand why in Session 6 on piping!
:::

```{r}
#| include: false
(Dat <- mutate(Dat,                                    # Use the Dat tibble.
              incc = incc - mean(incc),                # Transform to deviation from average.
              z_incc = incc / sd(incc),                # z-standardize incc.
              eastwest = fct_recode(eastwest,          # Recode eastwest.
                                 "Alte Bundeslaender" = "West", # "West" to "Alte Bundeslaender".
                                 "Neue Bundeslaender" = "Ost")  # "Ost" to "Neue Bundeslaender".
              ) # Don't forget to close mutate's bracket ")"
 )
```

```r
(Dat <- mutate(Dat,                                    # Use the Dat tibble.
              incc = incc - mean(incc),                # Transform to deviation from average.
              z_incc = incc / sd(incc),                # z-standardize incc.
              eastwest = fct_recode(eastwest,          # Recode eastwest.
                                 "Alte Bundeslaender" = "West", # "West" to "Alte Bundeslaender".
                                 "Neue Bundeslaender" = "Ost")  # "Ost" to "Neue Bundeslaender".
              ) # Don't forget to close mutate's bracket ")"
 )
```

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
Dat
```
:::

::: {.note}
Also, look how RStudio structures the brackets. It helps you to understand, within which function things are happening.
:::

## Conditional transform & recode ((i.e., for filtered cases))

To transform/recode only among certain cases, use `case_when()`.

```{r}
#| include: false
(Dat <- mutate(
  Dat, # Mutate variables contained in Dat.
  sex = case_when( # Start conditional recode of sex,
    eastwest == "Neue Bundeslaender" & incc < 0 ~ "Divers", # 1. complex condition ~ new value "Divers",
    age < 0 & id03 < 1          ~ "Keine Angabe",           # 2. complex condition ~ new value "Keine Angabe",
    TRUE ~ as.character(sex)                                # 3. and all others ~ leave as is;
  ) # close case_when's bracket.
)) # close mutate's (and the print) bracket
```

```r
(Dat <- mutate(
  Dat, # Mutate variables contained in Dat.
  sex = case_when( # Start conditional recode of sex,
    eastwest == "Neue Bundeslaender" & incc < 0 ~ "Divers", # 1. complex condition ~ new value "Divers",
    age < 0 & id03 < 1          ~ "Keine Angabe",           # 2. complex condition ~ new value "Keine Angabe",
    TRUE ~ as.character(sex)                                # 3. and all others ~ leave as is;
  ) # close case_when's bracket.
)) # close mutate's (and the print) bracket
```

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
Dat
```
:::

## Conditional transform & recode ((i.e., for filtered cases))

```{r eval = FALSE}
(Dat <- mutate(
  Dat, # Mutate variables contained in Dat.
  sex = case_when( # Start conditional recode of sex,
    eastwest == "Neue Bundeslaender" & incc < 0 ~ "Divers", # 1. complex condition ~ new value "Divers",
    age < 0 & id03 < 1          ~ "Keine Angabe",           # 2. complex condition ~ new value "Keine Angabe",
    TRUE ~ as.character(sex)                                # 3. and all others ~ leave as is;
  ) # close case_when's bracket.
)) # close mutate's (and the print) bracket .
```

The three lines of this `case_when()` application do the following thing:

1. For all cases from the Neue Bundeslaender with a below-average income ~ recode sex to "Divers".
2. For all those who're younger than 0 and score below 1 on the Oben-Unten-Skala ~ recode sex to "Keine Angabe".
3. All remaining cases ~ use their original sex values, but transform them to a character vector.
 - Remember, R is class sensitive! It will not combine numeric information into a character vector. Because we give `case_when()` `"Divers"` and `"Keine Angabe"` as new values, it assumes that we want to make sex a character vector. Thus we cannot supply the former factor values (which are integer) in line three.

## `case_when()` and `NA`

```r
(Dat <- mutate(
  Dat,
  sex = case_when( # Start conditional recode of sex,
    eastwest == "Neue Bundeslaender" & incc < 0 ~ "Divers", # 1. complex condition ~ new value "Divers",
    age < 0 & id03 < 1          ~ "Keine Angabe",           # 2. complex condition ~ new value "Keine Angabe",
    TRUE ~ NA_real_                     # 3. and all others ~ NA
  ) # close case_when's bracket.
))
```

::: {.fragment}
```{r error = TRUE}
(Dat <- mutate(
  Dat,
  sex = case_when( # Start conditional recode of sex,
    eastwest == "Neue Bundeslaender" & incc < 0 ~ "Divers", # 1. complex condition ~ new value "Divers",
    age < 0 & id03 < 1          ~ "Keine Angabe",           # 2. complex condition ~ new value "Keine Angabe",
    TRUE ~ NA_real_                     # 3. and all others ~ NA
  ) # close case_when's bracket.
))
```
:::

In R vectors are type sensitive; the elements of one vector may only be of one type. Because we give `case_when()` `"Divers"` and `"Keine Angabe"` as new values, it wants to make sex a character vector. But `NA` is a *logical* constant, and `NA_real_` a *numeric* one — neither combines with character values. If you type `?NA`, you will learn:

> "*NA is a logical* constant of length 1 which contains a missing value indicator. *NA can be coerced to any other vector type* except raw."

## `case_when()` and `NA`

`NA` are type sensitive, too! Therefore, coerce NA to character/numeric with `as.character()`/`as.numeric()`.

```{r error = TRUE}
#| include: false
(Dat <- mutate(
  Dat,
  sex = case_when( # Start conditional recode of sex,
    eastwest == "Neue Bundeslaender" & incc < 0 ~ "Divers", # 1. complex condition ~ new value "Divers",
    age < 0 & id03 < 1          ~ "Keine Angabe",           # 2. complex condition ~ new value "Keine Angabe",
    TRUE ~ as.character(NA)                              # 3. and all others ~ NA
  ) # close case_when's bracket.
)) # close mutate's (and the print) bracket.
```

```r
(Dat <- mutate(
  Dat,
  sex = case_when( # Start conditional recode of sex,
    eastwest == "Neue Bundeslaender" & incc < 0 ~ "Divers", # 1. complex condition ~ new value "Divers",
    age < 0 & id03 < 1          ~ "Keine Angabe",           # 2. complex condition ~ new value "Keine Angabe",
    TRUE ~ as.character(NA)                              # 3. and all others ~ NA
  ) # close case_when's bracket.
)) # close mutate's (and the print) bracket.
```

::: {.fragment}
```{r error = TRUE}
Dat
```
:::

::: {.note}
Alternatively, you can also use type-specific `NA`: `NA_character_`, `NA_real_`, etc..
:::

## Importing labelled data!

::: {.column width="50%"}
R imports Stata and SPSS labels, but cannot handle them. Thus, when you import Stata or SPSS data,<br>
... you need to change each labelled variable to **numeric or factor** from the outset of your analysis!!
:::

## Importing labelled data!

::: {.column width="50%"}
If you want to use a variable as categorical, use `as_factor()` to make the labels the new factor levels:
```{r comment = '#', eval = FALSE}
# Make the labelled sex variable a factor.
genderdata$sex <- as_factor(genderdata$sex)

# A frequency table to get a first impression of the variables values and frequencies.
table(genderdata$sex)
```
:::

## Importing labelled data!

::: {.column width="50%"}
If you want to use a variable as numeric, use `zap_labels()` to prohibit problems with the imported labels:

```{r comment = '#', eval = FALSE}
# Strip/zap the labels from the numeric variable age.
genderdata$age <- zap_labels(genderdata$age)

# A summary of descriptive statistics to get a first impression of the variable.
summary(genderdata$age)
```
:::

## Today's general lessons

1. *Data frames* organize equally-sized vectors along their indices; *Tibbles* are modernized data frames. The indices of data frames/tibbles are organized as `[row, column]`.
2. *Helper functions* are sub-functions that help you to make coding easier in many ways. They only work within the confines of the function for which they were designed as helpers.
3. Addressing variables means to address the columns of a data frame. Filtering cases means to address certain rows. Both is possible via the index `[row, column]`, but the `filter()` and `select()` functions have advantages.
4. R has no labels. The idea is that numeric variables have a scale (e.g., cm, years, DKK), while categorical variables have no true representation in numbers. When you import labelled data from Stata or SPSS, the labels are stored in R but will create confusion in the mid run. Make sure to `zap_labels()` from numeric variables and to treat categorical variables `as_factor()`.

## Today's important operators

1. `$`: Allows your to address vectors contained in a data frame/tibble.

## Today's (important) functions

1. `data.frame()`: organize several vectors of equal length by their index.
2. `as_tibble()`: take a data frame and make it a Tibble.
3. `read_rds()`: import an R data file (.rds) into your session.
4. `summary()`: Give a summary of an object.
5. `select()`: select several variables from a data frame/Tibble.
6. `filter()`: filter cases based on values in certain variables.
7. `mutate()`: Adds new variables and preserves existing. Good for recoding several variables.
8. `case_when()`: Conditional recode for cases filtered in complex ways.
9. `as_factor()`: Make a labelled Stata/SPSS variable a factor.
10. `zap_labels()`: Make a labelled Stata/SPSS variable numeric.
